questions.q: What is 'structural drift,' per this lesson?
options: A column gets renamed, resized, or dropped, and the documentation still describes the old shape
A column's business meaning changes while its structure stays the same
A table is backed up to a different server
A glossary term is marked as deprecated
questions.explain: Structural drift is a mismatch between the real schema and what's documented — directly detectable by comparing the two.

questions.q: Why can structural drift be caught automatically, per this lesson?
options: Because INFORMATION_SCHEMA is always current by definition, so the live schema and documented schema can be directly compared
Because SQL Server emails administrators whenever a column changes
Because structural drift never actually happens in real databases
Because extended properties automatically update themselves
questions.explain: A query comparing the live schema against documented columns produces an unambiguous, automatic signal when the two disagree.

questions.q: What is 'descriptive drift,' as distinct from structural drift?
options: The column's business meaning shifts while the schema itself stays unchanged, so nothing signals the drift automatically
A column is physically deleted from the database
A table's name is changed without updating any code
A database is migrated to a new server
questions.explain: Descriptive drift happens when what a column means in practice changes (like a business redefining 'active' from 90 to 60 days) without any change to the schema itself.

questions.q: In the worked ShippingStatus example, why didn't a structural-drift query catch the new 'Returned' value?
options: Because the column's schema (a VARCHAR type) never changed — only its practical set of values did, invisibly to the schema
Because the query had a syntax error
Because 'Returned' was added to a completely different, unrelated table
Because INFORMATION_SCHEMA does not support VARCHAR columns
questions.explain: The column was still a VARCHAR before and after — nothing in the schema itself reflects that a new valid value started appearing in the data.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the only real defense against descriptive drift?
options: A scheduled review where the accountable owner actively re-confirms the description still matches current business meaning
Running the structural-drift SQL query more frequently
Deleting the column and recreating it
There is no defense — descriptive drift cannot ever be prevented or caught
questions.explain: This connects back to the 'last reviewed' field from Lesson 3 — a periodic, deliberate human check is the only way to catch a meaning that has quietly shifted.
